patient.chief_complaint: Sudden-onset severe dysphagia with bilateral loss of gag reflex, no limb weakness, aspiration pneumonia, and 9 kg weight loss over 2 weeks.
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. L. is a 74-year-old retired librarian presenting with a 2-week history of progressive dysphagia. She developed sudden-onset difficulty swallowing during meals, with frequent episodes of aspiration and nasal regurgitation on large boluses. Her hoarse voice developed during the same period. She has been unable to eat adequately resulting in a 9 kg weight loss over 2 weeks. This is her second episode — 3 years ago she had a transient episode of dysphagia that resolved spontaneously without diagnosis. She denied any recent vaccinations or infections prior to this episode. She has no limb weakness, no sensory symptoms, and no facial weakness. Laryngoscopy shows normal vocal cord movement. CT chest confirms aspiration pneumonia in the right lower lobe. Brain MRI shows no new lesions and the prior PCA territory infarction is chronic. Contrast-enhanced CT neck shows no structural obstruction. The bilateral loss of gag reflex with dysphagia in the absence of limb weakness raises the question of a bulbar GBS variant — specifically the pharyngeal-cervical-brachial (PCB) variant or isolated bulbar GBS. The anti-GT1a antibody — which is not widely available — would be the key serological marker. Serial electrophysiological studies will be needed to assess NMJ function and look for nerve involvement.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, isolated bulbar variant with anti-GT1a IgG antibodies (pharyngeal-cervical-brachial bulbar subtype)

differential.key_features: AChR/MuSK negative; RNS no decrement; no ptosis or fatigability
No craniobulbar denervation on EMG — paraspinal denervation without bulbar denervation excludes bulbar ALS; acute onset inconsistent with ALS
MRI DWI negative for new stroke; bilateral CN IX-X enhancement on MRI confirms peripheral GBS
Normal tumor markers; CSF no malignant cells; NCS pattern not paraneoplastic

optimal_actions.expected_finding: No new stroke; CN IX-X enhancement — GBS

optimal_actions.action: NCS/EMG with RNS and bulbar EMG
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Isolated bulbar neuronopathy; normal limb NCS; no NMJ decrement; no craniobulbar denervation

NGT placement — NPO for aspiration risk; nutritional support

critical_actions: Anti-GT1a antibody is the key serological marker for bulbar/PCB GBS — not included in standard ganglioside panels; requires send-out testing
NPO status is mandatory — bilateral gag loss with aspiration on VFSS means oral intake is unsafe regardless of GBS treatment
Aspiration pneumonia requires antibiotic treatment concurrent with IVIG — dual management needed
Motor neuron disease excluded by absence of craniobulbar denervation on EMG — this is the critical EMG finding that rules out bulbar ALS
Prior stroke history (9 years ago, no deficits) is not related — new bilateral cranial nerve involvement is GBS, not stroke recurrence
key_reasoning_points: Isolated bulbar GBS: dysphagia without limb weakness is a recognized GBS variant — anti-GT1a antibody syndrome affecting oropharyngeal nerves preferentially
Anti-GT1a is not on standard ganglioside panels — must specifically request or use a send-out reference lab
Bilateral gag reflex loss with dysphagia is the key cranial nerve finding — bilateral CN IX-X palsy in acute onset is GBS until proven otherwise
The prior episode 3 years ago that resolved spontaneously may represent a prior GBS bulbar variant — recurrent GBS occurs in ~5% of cases
Paraspinal denervation on EMG without craniobulbar denervation specifically excludes motor neuron disease — this EMG distinction is important
